summary: Explains why separate Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) need to work together. Network operators increasingly run their own CDNs, and interconnecting them could extend reach, improve delivery quality, and cut costs. The document lays out the problem and the areas where standard interfaces would be needed. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6707 describes why content delivery networks may need to work together to serve users. It names four interfaces for coordinating delivery, while leaving the transfer of content itself outside the work it describes.

questions: what are the four cdni interfaces
subtitle: Why separate content delivery networks need agreed ways to hand off delivery work.

tldr.problem: A CDN may not have enough reach or capacity to serve every user, and the RFC found no open specifications for CDN-to-CDN interconnection.
tldr.mechanism: The problem statement identifies four interfaces: Control, Request Routing, Metadata, and Logging, and discusses reuse of existing protocols.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational problem statement that scoped IETF work. It defines no CDNI protocol, and content transfer between CDNs is outside its scope.

today: RFC 6707 is an Informational problem statement published in September 2012. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it framed the CDNI problem area and defined no protocol.

sections.title: Why Interconnect CDNs
sections.content:
A content delivery network (CDN) can place cacheable content closer to users, reduce delivery costs, improve quality of experience, and increase delivery robustness. A single CDN may not have a nearby footprint or enough resources for every request, so providers may want to use another CDN to serve some requests.

In the model described, a content service provider has an arrangement with an authoritative CDN. That CDN may delegate delivery to a downstream CDN. The commercial arrangements are outside this RFC's scope; the technical problem is the lack of open specifications for interconnection.
sections.plainLanguage: One CDN may not have servers or resources close enough to every user. The RFC describes how one CDN could ask another to deliver some content on its behalf.

sections.title: CDN Roles and a Delivery Request
sections.content:
The authoritative CDN has a direct relationship with the content service provider. For a given request, the upstream CDN redirects it to a downstream CDN. A surrogate is the cache that delivers content to the user's software.

The upstream CDN may serve the request itself or redirect it. The user's software follows the redirect and requests the content from the downstream CDN. If needed, that CDN acquires the content from the upstream CDN, which may in turn obtain it from the content service provider.
sections.plainLanguage: The upstream CDN can redirect a request to a downstream CDN that can serve it. The downstream CDN may need to obtain the content before it can reply.

sections.title: Four Interfaces in the Problem Area
sections.content:
The RFC describes four use cases, including independent CDNs run by related providers, content providers seeking broad reach, separate CDNs for different services, and an over-the-top CDN using another CDN for operational or commercial reasons. It identifies four interfaces between a pair of CDNs.

  • Control: bootstraps and configures the other interfaces, shares capabilities, and can request actions such as pre-positioning or purging.
  • Request Routing: supports redirection and sharing footprint or capability information.
  • Metadata: carries delivery rules such as geographic restrictions, availability windows, and access controls.
  • Logging: transfers activity records used for charging, reporting, or monitoring.

The interface grouping is tentative in this problem statement.
sections.plainLanguage: The four interfaces coordinate setup, request redirection, delivery rules, and activity records. The RFC treats these groups as a starting point, not a final design.

sections.title: Reusing Existing Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC treats all four interfaces as application-layer control-plane functions and recommends building on existing protocols rather than creating a new application protocol. It gives HTTP, the Atom Publishing Protocol, and XMPP as examples, while making clear that the examples do not decide what the working group must use.

It describes request-response services as possible for routing and metadata, existing routing or ALTO mechanisms as possible for footprint information, and SNMP, syslog, FTP, or HTTP POST as candidates for logging. The control interface was less clearly defined than the other three.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC suggests that existing Internet protocols could carry the interface messages. Its examples are possibilities, not a final choice.

sections.title: Trust and Privacy Across CDNs
sections.content:
Interconnection extends trust from a content provider to one CDN and then to another. Existing safeguards may still help, but their suitability in a multi-CDN chain needs validation. Different legal regimes may also limit what information can be shared; downstream logging may need to remove or anonymize some fields.

The interfaces have distinct risks. A compromised Control interface could affect the others. A rogue upstream CDN could send bogus requests, while a rogue downstream CDN could influence redirection. Metadata needs peer authentication, and logs may contain sensitive information or support charging.
sections.plainLanguage: Each CDN must decide which other CDNs it trusts and what information it can share. The RFC identifies risks to requests, delivery rules, logs, and interface configuration.
